lessonPlan.title: The Minister's Black Veil unit
lessonPlan.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
lessonPlan.editionNote: Reading text: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Twice-Told_Tales_(1837)/The_Minister's_Black_Veil (revision 9901756), cleaned for Liber et Libri.
lessonPlan.gradeBand: Grades 10–12 (scales to graduate via rigor levels)

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this story, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in The Minister's Black Veil.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about The Minister's Black Veil: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

lessonPlan.middleSchoolTrack: Short story: read whole in one 90-minute lesson (assign longer stories as pre-reading). Middle School prompts use the full text when the grade tags include 6–8; otherwise teacher-selected passages.
lessonPlan.schedule: One 90-minute lesson (the whole story), with an optional take-home essay
essentialQuestions: What does The Minister's Black Veil suggest about secret sin?
What does The Minister's Black Veil suggest about isolation?
What does The Minister's Black Veil suggest about symbol and meaning?
objectives: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly and implicitly.
Determine themes and analyze their development over the course of the story.
Analyze how characters, setting and point of view interact.
Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in the text.
Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.

wholeBookTest.title: The Minister's Black Veil: whole-book test

options: A black veil over his face

items.prompt: What happens at the young lady's funeral?
options: Some fancy the corpse shudders as Hooper bends over it

items.prompt: What effect does the veil have on his ministry?
options: He becomes powerful with sinners but feared

items.prompt: What does Hooper say on his deathbed?
options: He sees a black veil on every face

items.prompt: In the line “A person, who watched the interview between the dead and living, scrupled not to affirm, that, at the instant when the clergyman's features were disclosed, the corpse had slightly shuddered, rustling the shroud and muslin cap, though the countenance retained the composure of death.”, what does “scrupled” most nearly mean?
options: speak, pronounce, or utter in a certain way
hesitated because of a moral doubt

items.prompt: In the line “Hooper, a gentlemanly person of about thirty, though still a bachelor, was dressed with due clerical neatness, as if a careful wife had starched his band, and brushed the weekly dust from his Sunday's garb.”, what does “neatness” most nearly mean?
options: hesitated because of a moral doubt
speak, pronounce, or utter in a certain way

items.prompt: As used in the story (“A person, who watched the interview between the dead and living, scrupled not to affirm, that, at the instant when the clergyman's features ”), what does “scrupled” mean?
options: hesitated because of a moral doubt

items.prompt: As used in the story (“Hooper, a gentlemanly person of about thirty, though still a bachelor, was dressed with due clerical neatness, as if a careful wife had star”), what does “neatness” mean?
options: pause or hold back in uncertainty or unwillingness

items.prompt: As used in the story (“Hooper's mildness did not forsake him.”), what does “mildness” mean?
options: be larger in number, quantity, power, status or importance
speak, pronounce, or utter in a certain way

items.prompt: As used in the story (“Finally, the deputies returned abashed to their constituents, pronouncing the matter too weighty to be handled, except by a council of the c”), what does “pronouncing” mean?
options: hesitated because of a moral doubt
speak, pronounce, or utter in a certain way

items.prompt: As used in the story (“For a few moments she appeared lost in thought, considering, probably, what new methods might be tried, to withdraw her lover from so dark a”), what does “symptom” mean?
options: pause or hold back in uncertainty or unwillingness

shortAnswer: Explain how secret sin develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
Explain how isolation develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
Explain how symbol and meaning develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
wholeBookTest.essay: Choose one of the story's central concerns (secret sin, isolation, symbol and meaning) and argue how the ending reframes it.

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track): write a five-paragraph essay explaining what The Minister's Black Veil teaches about secret sin. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Nathaniel Hawthorne develops secret sin in The Minister's Black Veil. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Nathaniel Hawthorne develops secret sin across The Minister's Black Veil. Trace the idea through at least three parts of the story and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of The Minister's Black Veil (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of secret sin. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of secret sin in The Minister's Black Veil. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how Nathaniel Hawthorne's choices in The Minister's Black Veil (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of secret sin, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places The Minister's Black Veil's treatment of secret sin in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on secret sin in The Minister's Black Veil that reads the story against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on secret sin in The Minister's Black Veil. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about secret sin in The Minister's Black Veil, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on secret sin in The Minister's Black Veil, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.
